subject: Cognitive Science
title: How Children Learn Word Meanings
description: A fast breakdown of How Children Learn Word Meanings for builders.

hook.text: A toddler hears "dog" while seeing a dog, a ball, and a tree. How does she know which one?

buildup.text: Quine called this the problem of induction—infinite possible meanings for any new word.

discovery.text: Children use constraints: whole-object bias means a new label probably names the whole thing.

twist.text: Mutual exclusivity helps too—if she already knows "ball," a new word must label something else.

climax.text: These biases act as shortcuts that make the impossible task of word learning tractable.

punchline.text: Kids don't guess randomly—they guess smart.

quiz.question: What is the whole-object bias in word learning?
options: Children assume a new word labels the whole object

details.summary: Children learn word meanings at astonishing speed through biases like the whole-object assumption, mutual exclusivity, and shape bias. These constraints narrow the infinite possible meanings a new word could have. By age six, children know roughly 14,000 words, learning several new ones daily.
details.whyItMatters: The speed of word learning is one of the most remarkable feats of human development. Understanding the biases that make it possible illuminates both language and cognition.
takeaways: Children use constraints to narrow possible word meanings
The whole-object assumption maps labels to entire objects first
By age six children know approximately 14,000 words

faq.question: What is fast mapping?
faq.answer: Fast mapping is the ability to create an initial word-object connection from a single exposure. A child hearing a novel word like chromium in context picks up its rough meaning immediately. Full understanding deepens over repeated encounters, but the initial link forms remarkably quickly.

faq.question: What is the mutual exclusivity constraint?
faq.answer: Children assume each object has one label. If they already know the word cup and hear a new word next to a cup and an unfamiliar object, they map the new word to the novel object. This constraint dramatically speeds up vocabulary acquisition by eliminating ambiguity.
